claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native iron-oxide layer in its pre-exposure state.
At room temperature, Q235 steel's corrosion resistance arises from a coherent protective iron-oxide scale.
The room-temperature oxide scale limits ion transport and further corrosion.
The protective scale on Q235 steel may comprise Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
Exposure at 700–900 °C drives phase transformations relevant to corrosion protection.
High-temperature exposure increases diffusion in the Q235 oxide scale.
High-temperature diffusion and thermal stresses promote oxide-scale coarsening.
High-temperature diffusion and thermal stresses promote mechanical spallation of the oxide scale.
Oxide-scale transformation, coarsening, and spallation expose fresh Q235 steel.
Exposure of fresh steel following scale disruption causes accelerated corrosive attack.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, high-temperature exposure will produce detectable changes in oxide phase composition by XRD.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, high-temperature exposure will produce lower impedance.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, high-temperature exposure will produce a higher corrosion current.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, high-temperature exposure will produce greater mass loss.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, high-temperature exposure will produce more visibly spalled oxide regions.
At room temperature, the oxide scale remains intact and corrosion indicators are minimal under the selected salt exposure.
The proposed mechanism is limited to as-received Q235 steel and need not apply to pre-annealed or HEA-coated specimens.
Temperature will be varied while salt composition, exposure duration, and atmospheric conditions are held constant.
